hints: Think about what particles are present in solid ammonium chloride after proton transfer from HCl to NH3.
Recall how a coordinate bond differs from a normal covalent bond in terms of where both shared electrons come from.
walkthrough:
Picture what proton transfer creates**
When $\text{NH}_3$ meets $\text{HCl}$, the $\text{H}^+$ moves onto the lone pair on N. You are left with a tetrahedral $\text{NH}_4^+$ cation and a $\text{Cl}^-$ anion. In the solid these opposite ions attract electrostatically, and that is your ionic bonding.

Sort the bonds inside the cation**
Inside $\text{NH}_4^+$, N is joined to four H atoms by four shared pairs, so all four look like covalent bonds. The key difference is origin: three were normal $\text{N-H}$ bonds already in $\text{NH}_3$, while the fourth was formed when both electrons came from N to bond to $\text{H}^+$. Show that one with an arrow pointing from N to H to flag the coordinate bond.

Final answer: Show $\text{NH}_4^+$ ion with 4 $\text{N-H}$ covalent bonds surrounding N and $\text{Cl}^-$ ion alongside, with ionic attraction between $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$.
One $\text{N-H}$ bond shown as a coordinate bond, e.g. arrow from N to H, with the other three as normal shared pairs.

hints: Focus on what $\text{NH}_4^+$ can donate and what $\text{OH}^-$ can accept when they meet in water.
walkthrough:
Spot the proton transfer**
$\text{NH}_4^+$ is the conjugate acid of $\text{NH}_3$ and readily donates $\text{H}^+$, while $\text{OH}^-$ readily accepts $\text{H}^+$. A reaction by proton transfer between an acid and a base is an acid-base reaction.

hints: Start with $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ as reactants and think which two neutral molecules they can form by moving one proton.
walkthrough:
Build the ionic equation**
Let $\text{OH}^-$ remove one $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{NH}_4^+$. $$\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Atoms and charges balance: one N, five H, one O and zero net charge on each side.

hints: Remember the name given to a species that uses a lone pair to attack an electron deficient carbon.
walkthrough:
Link lone pair to role**
Both $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{OH}^-$ use a lone pair to form a new bond to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of the halogenoalkane. A lone pair donor to an electron deficient centre is a nucleophile.

hints: Compare a neutral molecule with a lone pair against a negatively charged ion with lone pairs attacking the same $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ centre.
walkthrough:
Weigh charge attraction**
Picture $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ or a full $\text{C}^+$. A full negative charge on $\text{OH}^-$ gives stronger electrostatic attraction to that positive carbon than neutral $\text{NH}_3$ does, so $\text{OH}^-$ is expected to attack faster. The alternative accepted argument is that N in $\text{NH}_3$ is less electronegative than O, so its lone pair is less tightly held and more easily donated.
Final answer: $\text{OH}^-$ is more reactive because the negatively charged ion is more strongly attracted to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ / carbocation intermediate.

hints: Recall how many steps and intermediates appear in SN1 compared with the single concerted step in SN2.
Think how the height of the energy barrier must compare if the SN2 route is described as slower with the same reactants and products.
walkthrough:
Keep start and finish fixed**
Both mechanisms convert the same reactants to the same products, so your new curve must start on the same reactants level and end on the same products level as the printed SN1 curve.

Show one step with a higher barrier**
SN1 has two humps with an intermediate valley because bond breaking and bond making occur in separate steps. SN2 is concerted, so draw one smooth hump with no valley. Because SN2 is slower, its activation energy is larger, so the top of your single hump must sit higher than both SN1 peaks.

Final answer: Single hump curve starting at same reactants energy and finishing at same products energy as SN1 curve.
Peak (transition state) higher than both SN1 peaks, showing larger activation energy for slower SN2 reaction.

hints: Start with the polar $\text{C-Br}$ bond in 2-bromobutane and decide which way the bonding electrons move when the carbocation forms.
Identify the lone pair on $\text{NH}_3$ and the positive carbon it will attack in the second step.
Look at the $\text{N}^+$ intermediate in the third structure and think where the $\text{N-H}$ bonding electrons must go to give the neutral amine.
walkthrough:
Break the carbon bromine bond**
Mark the $\text{C-Br}$ bond as $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ because Br is more electronegative. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-Br}$ bond onto Br. That heterolysis ejects $\text{Br}^-$ and leaves the planar secondary carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}^+\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ shown in Fig. 4.2.

Attack with ammonia**
Show a lone pair on N in $\text{NH}_3$. Draw a curly arrow from that lone pair to the $\text{C}^+$. This forms the $\text{C-N}$ bond and gives the $\text{H}_3\text{N}^+-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)$ intermediate with positive charge on N.

Remove the extra proton**
The $\text{N}^+$ still carries an extra H. Draw a curly arrow from one $\text{N}^+-\text{H}$ bond back onto N. That pair becomes the N lone pair, releasing $\text{H}^+$ and leaving neutral $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$.

Final answer: On $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrC}_2\text{H}_5$: $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown and curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to Br to form $\text{Br}^-$ and secondary carbocation.
Curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{NH}_3$ to $\text{C}^+$ to form $\text{C-N}^+$ bond.
Curly arrow from $\text{N}^+-\text{H}$ bond to N in final deprotonation step.

hints: Combine the $\text{H}^+$ released in the last step with the $\text{Br}^-$ released in the first step, remembering excess $\text{NH}_3$ is present.
walkthrough:
Track the leftover ions**
Heterolysis gave $\text{Br}^-$ and deprotonation gave $\text{H}^+$. In ammonia solution $\text{H}^+ + \text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+$, so the inorganic salt isolated is $\text{NH}_4\text{Br}$.
Final answer: $\text{NH}_4\text{Br}$ / ammonium bromide

hints: Count the longest carbon chain containing the $\text{NH}_2$ group and number it to give the amine the lowest locant.
walkthrough:
Name the amine**
$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ has a four carbon chain with $\text{NH}_2$ on carbon 2. The systematic name is butan-2-amine.

hints: Remove Br from 2-bromo-2-methylpropane as $\text{Br}^-$ and draw the carbon skeleton left with the positive charge.
walkthrough:
Draw the tertiary cation**
2-bromo-2-methylpropane is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$. Loss of $\text{Br}^-$ leaves $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$, a central $\text{C}^+$ joined to three $\text{CH}_3$ groups.
Final answer: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ / $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3^+$ with positive charge on central C

hints: Compare the carbocation from 2-bromobutane, which is secondary, with the carbocation from 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
Recall how alkyl groups push electron density toward a neighbouring positive charge.
walkthrough:
Pick the more stable cation**
2-bromobutane gives a secondary carbocation with two alkyl groups on $\text{C}^+$, while 2-bromo-2-methylpropane gives a tertiary carbocation with three alkyl groups on $\text{C}^+$. The tertiary cation is more stable, so 2-bromo-2-methylpropane has the greater tendency to react by SN1, where carbocation formation is the slow step.

Explain with the inductive effect**
Alkyl groups are electron donating by the positive inductive effect. More alkyl groups push more electron density onto the electron deficient $\text{C}^+$, spreading the positive charge and lowering energy. That extra stabilisation favours the SN1 pathway for the tertiary halogenoalkane.

Final answer: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, as it forms the more stable carbocation / $\text{C}^+$.
More alkyl groups attached to $\text{C}^+$ give a greater positive inductive effect, stabilising the carbocation more.
